prompt: Why does this course add a C compiler to the machine the `go` course built?
hint: Think about what the race detector is written in.

choices.text: Go 1.27.1 compiles goroutines through C
choices.why: Goroutines are ordinary Go and build with no C at all; `spin.go` would build on a machine with no `gcc`.

choices.text: The race detector is a C++ runtime that is linked in through cgo
choices.why: Right. `-race` links ThreadSanitizer through cgo, and cgo needs a C compiler on the machine.

choices.text: The `testing` package of lessons 25 to 30 is written in C
choices.why: `testing` is Go. Only the race detector needs cgo, and with it the compiler.

choices.text: `gofmt` refuses to format files when `gcc` is missing
choices.why: `gofmt` is a Go program with nothing to do with C. The section's check found it in `/usr/local/go/bin` beside `go`.

prompt: Ana runs `go env CGO_ENABLED CC` on a fresh machine and gets `1` and `gcc`. Nobody set either value. What does the `1` tell her?
hint: Section 05 shows the same command printing `0`.

choices.text: That one goroutine at a time is allowed to run
choices.why: That would be `GOMAXPROCS=1`, a different setting entirely.

choices.text: That the race detector is switched on for every build
choices.why: The detector is on only when `-race` is passed. `CGO_ENABLED` says whether it could be.

choices.text: The go command looked for `gcc` and found it
choices.why: Right. With no compiler in sight the default turns to `0`, as section 05 showed.

choices.text: That the installed Go is release 1 of the language
choices.why: `go version` reports the release, `go1.27.1`. `CGO_ENABLED` is a switch, on or off.

prompt: Why does the course recommend against learning it on the Go Playground, although the Playground runs Go programs?
hint: What does the course ask you to read, besides the program?

choices.text: There is no terminal to type `go run -race` or `go test` in
choices.why: Right. Half the course is reading what the go command prints, and the Playground gives you no go command to type.

choices.text: It runs a release of Go older than the one with `WaitGroup.Go`
choices.why: The section makes no claim about the Playground's release. Its objection is what is missing around the program.

choices.text: Goroutines are disabled there
choices.why: The section does not say so, and it recommends the Playground for trying fragments.

choices.text: It needs a paid account
choices.why: It costs nothing. The objection is the missing terminal.

prompt: A classmate has Go 1.27.1 in `/usr/local/go` and an old Go from a package manager in `/usr/bin`. Their `~/.profile` appends `/usr/local/go/bin` to the end of `PATH`. What does `go version` report?
hint: The shell runs the first match it finds, reading `PATH` from left to right.

choices.text: 1.27.1, because the newest release wins
choices.why: The shell knows nothing about releases. It takes the first `go` along `PATH`.

choices.text: The old release in `/usr/bin`
choices.why: Right. `/usr/bin` comes earlier in `PATH`, so its `go` runs. `command -v go` would name that file.

choices.text: An error, because two programs with the same name conflict
choices.why: Nothing conflicts: the shell stops at the first match and never sees the second.

choices.text: Both releases, one per line
choices.why: One program runs, and it prints one line.

prompt: In Rob Pike's terms, which of these is a property of the PROGRAM rather than of a run?
hint: One of the two words describes how the code is written.

choices.text: Parallelism
choices.why: Parallelism is whether, at an instant, more than one activity is executing. The same program had different amounts of it in three runs.

choices.text: Concurrency
choices.why: Right. It is how the program is structured, as independent activities, and it was the same in every run of `spin.go`.

choices.text: The number of processors
choices.why: That belongs to the machine, and `nproc` reports it.

choices.text: The value of `GOMAXPROCS`
choices.why: `GOMAXPROCS` was changed between runs without touching the source, so it belongs to the run.

prompt: `spin.go` took 400 ms with `GOMAXPROCS=4` and 1.57 s with `GOMAXPROCS=1`. Roughly how many times longer did the run with one processor take? Give a whole number.
hint: 1,570 divided by 400.

prompt: `wait.go` runs four goroutines that each sleep one second. With `GOMAXPROCS=1` it finished in one second, not four. Why?
hint: What does a sleeping goroutine need a processor for?

choices.text: `GOMAXPROCS` is ignored for sleeping goroutines
choices.why: It is not ignored; it is simply not a limit on anything that waits. It limits goroutines executing Go code.

choices.text: The runtime cut the sleeps short to save time
choices.why: Each sleep lasted its full second. They overlapped instead of running one after another.

choices.text: A sleeping goroutine needs no processor
choices.why: Right. While one waits there is nothing to run for it, and all four wait at once.

choices.text: The machine has four processors whatever `GOMAXPROCS` says
choices.why: `GOMAXPROCS=1` really did limit Go code to one processor: `spin.go` took 1.57 s with it.

prompt: A program fetches 200 web pages, one after another, and spends almost all its time waiting for the network. It runs on a one-processor machine. What does rewriting it with one goroutine per page buy?
hint: This is `wait.go` with a network in place of `time.Sleep`.

choices.text: Nothing, since one processor leaves no room for parallelism
choices.why: No parallelism, yes. But the waits overlap, as `wait.go` showed with `GOMAXPROCS=1`.

choices.text: Much less time on the clock, because the waits overlap
choices.why: Right. Concurrency pays even without parallelism when the work is mostly waiting.

choices.text: Roughly half the time, the most one processor allows
choices.why: There is no such ceiling for waiting: four one-second sleeps took one second, a quarter.

choices.text: Faster arithmetic in each request
choices.why: The arithmetic is the same and there is little of it. What changes is that waiting stops being sequential.

prompt: Match each run of `spin.go` with the time it printed.
hint: One processor took about four times as long as four.

prompt: `order.go` printed `caio` first in five runs out of five. What may a program built on it assume about the order of the greetings?
hint: Is the order part of the language, or of one release's scheduler?

choices.text: That `caio` comes first, since five runs agreed
choices.why: Five agreeing runs describe this scheduler on this machine. The `-race` build of the same program printed `ana` first.

choices.text: That they come in the order the loop started them
choices.why: The loop started `ana` first, and `ana` was last in four of the five runs.

choices.text: Nothing: the order is not part of the language
choices.why: Right. If order matters, the program has to impose it, with a channel or a lock.

choices.text: That they come in alphabetical order
choices.why: The runs printed `caio`, `ana`, `bia`, which is not alphabetical, and nothing sorts goroutines.

prompt: One of the five runs of `count.go` printed `total: 400000`, the right answer. Why does the lesson call that the most dangerous line on the screen?
hint: Imagine a test that ran the program once.

choices.text: One run like it passes a test with the race still inside
choices.why: Right. The defect is in the program whether or not a given run shows it.

choices.text: It proves that the race detector was switched off for that one run
choices.why: It was switched off, since these runs had no `-race`, but a right total proves nothing about the detector.

choices.text: It overflows an `int` and wraps around
choices.why: 400,000 fits an `int` with room to spare. Lost updates make the total smaller, never larger.

choices.text: It means two goroutines never started
choices.why: If two had never started the total would be at most 200,000.

prompt: Put the steps of the lost update in the lesson's figure in order. `total` starts at 7.
hint: Both reads happen before either write.

prompt: Which of these make something one goroutine did visible to another, by Go's promises? Choose all that apply.
hint: Go's promises are about synchronisation, not about timing.

choices.text: A value sent on a channel and received by the other
choices.why: Yes. What the sender did before the send is visible to the receiver after the receive.

choices.text: `wg.Wait` returning after the goroutine finished
choices.why: Yes. That is why `count.go` may read `total` after `wg.Wait`.

choices.text: Waiting long enough with `time.Sleep`
choices.why: A sleep is timing, not synchronisation. Go promises nothing about what a pause makes visible.

choices.text: Both goroutines writing to the same variable
choices.why: That is the data race itself, the thing the promises do not cover.

prompt: `go run -race count.go` printed two race reports and a wrong total. A colleague runs the race detector once over a program and sees no report. What can they conclude?
hint: What does the detector watch?

choices.text: That the program has no data race
choices.why: The detector reports races that happen in the run it watches. A path the run never took is unexamined.

choices.text: That no race happened on the paths that run took
choices.why: Right. It is evidence about one run, which is why lesson 16 runs it over tests that exercise the code.

choices.text: That the detector was not linked in
choices.why: If `-race` could not be linked, the go command refuses with `-race requires cgo` rather than staying quiet.

choices.text: That the program will print the same output every time
choices.why: Even a race-free program like `order.go` prints its lines in different orders.

prompt: A program run with the race detector that finds a race exits with status ___, so a script can notice.
hint: The last line of the `go run -race count.go` transcript.

prompt: On a machine with no C compiler, `go run -race` says `-race requires cgo; enable cgo by setting CGO_ENABLED=1`. What happens if the student does exactly that?
hint: Section 05 tried it.

choices.text: The program runs, with the race detector inside it
choices.why: cgo still needs a compiler to build the C half of the runtime, and there is none.

choices.text: It fails one step later, naming the missing `gcc`
choices.why: Right: `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found`. The repair is to install the compiler.

choices.text: The go command downloads a C compiler from the module proxy
choices.why: The module proxy serves Go modules and toolchains. A C compiler comes from your system's packages.

choices.text: The same message again, word for word
choices.why: The message changes: it now names the compiler it looked for.

prompt: A student has `gcc` installed and `command -v gcc` finds it, yet `go test -race` still says `-race requires cgo`. Where should they look first?
hint: If the compiler is there, the switch was turned off by somebody.

choices.text: Reinstall Go, because the toolchain is damaged
choices.why: Nothing points at the toolchain. The message is about cgo being off.

choices.text: Install a second C compiler such as `clang`
choices.why: The first compiler is found. Another would change nothing while cgo is switched off.

choices.text: `go env -changed`, looking for `CGO_ENABLED=0`
choices.why: Right. It lists every setting that differs from the default, whether it came from the shell or from `go env -w`.

choices.text: Lower `GOMAXPROCS` to 1
choices.why: `GOMAXPROCS` decides parallelism and has nothing to do with cgo.

prompt: Match each message with its cause.
hint: Two of them come from the go command and one from the shell.

pairs.right: cgo is off, by default or by hand
cgo forced on with no compiler installed

right_distractors: two goroutines wrote the same variable

prompt: Put the lab's checks in the order section 02 ran them, from the toolchain outwards.
hint: The race check comes last, because it needs everything before it.

prompt: A team moves its service from a four-processor machine to a container limited to one processor. Its requests mostly wait on a database. Which of the lesson's two programs predicts what happens to it?
hint: Is the service's time spent computing or waiting?

choices.text: `spin.go`: it will take about four times as long
choices.why: That is the prediction for work that computes. This service mostly waits.

choices.text: `wait.go`: waiting overlaps on a single processor as well
choices.why: Right. Requests that wait barely need the processor, so losing three of them costs far less than four times.

choices.text: `count.go`: one processor removes the data race
choices.why: A race does not need two processors: goroutines interleave on one as well, and the memory model makes no exception for it.

choices.text: `order.go`: the requests will be answered in order
choices.why: Nothing about one processor makes goroutines run in the order they were started.
